sections.html:
Houma is the largest city in Terrebonne Parish and its parish seat. Since 1984 the city government has been folded into the Terrebonne Parish Consolidated Government, so permits, planning and most local services come from the parish rather than a separate city hall.

The 2020 count was 33,406 people, and the July 1, 2025 estimate is 31,735, a decline. The city covers 14.47 square miles of land. Bayou Cane, the neighboring community that locals often treat as part of Houma, is counted separately. US Route 90, slated to become Interstate 49, plus Louisiana 24, 311 and 182 are the main roads.

Energy, marine work, seafood and health care drive the local economy, and oil prices and offshore activity can leave a household with a house to sell on short notice after a layoff or transfer. A buyer who can close on a firm date helps in that situation.

Houma is mostly owner-occupied. For 2020 to 2024, 72.4 percent of housing units are owned and the median home value is $205,900. Median monthly owner costs are $1,548 with a mortgage and $449 without. Median gross rent is $1,058, and the city has 13,346 households averaging 2.41 people.

Citywide figures like these say little about any one street, so treat them as background and ask for comparable sales near your address before settling on a price.

sections.h2: How did Hurricane Ida affect Houma houses?
sections.html:
Hurricane Ida made landfall in southeast Louisiana on August 29, 2021, and Houma took the intense eye wall of the Category 4 storm. Widespread damage followed, and displacement and property damage lingered long afterward. Statewide, more than 564,000 individual assistance applications were approved for over $1.2 billion, 14,540 flood insurance claims were paid for more than $655 million and over 26,000 Small Business Administration disaster loan applications came in. Those are state totals, not Houma figures, but they show how big the repair and insurance process was.

If your house was hit, buyers tend to ask:

  • Was the roof replaced, and was the work permitted?
  • Was there wind-driven water inside the walls or attic?
  • Did an insurance or FEMA payment cover the repairs, and were the repairs finished?
  • Are there leftover blue tarps, rotted decking or mold?

An as-is buyer who does not need a lender's appraisal can often close despite open repairs, which is why damaged houses sometimes sell this way.

FEMA has been revising the flood maps for portions of Houma and unincorporated Terrebonne Parish, and revised preliminary maps came out on October 8, 2021. The maps define Special Flood Hazard Areas, which are high-risk areas, and they set flood insurance rates. You can view them through the local floodplain administrator, the FEMA Map Service Center online, a Flood Map Changes Viewer, or a Map Specialist at 1-877-FEMA-MAP (1-877-336-2627).

Preliminary maps are not final, so check the status for your address before telling a buyer what zone it is in. A seller can do three things:

  • Look up the effective map and any preliminary map for the address.
  • Keep any elevation certificate and flood insurance declarations page.
  • Be ready to say whether the house flooded in the past and how it was repaired.

sections.h2: What weather does a Houma house have to withstand?
sections.html:
Houma is low and wet, at about 10 feet above sea level, with 65.42 inches of rain in a normal year. July and August are the wettest months at 9.06 and 6.50 inches. Daily mean temperatures reach about 82.7 degrees in July and 82.9 in August, with record highs of 104, and a February record low of 5 degrees can split exposed pipes in a house that has not seen a deep freeze in years.

Buyers and inspectors focus on roofing, drainage and moisture. A recent roof, working gutters and a dry crawl space or slab edge usually mean fewer price questions.

sections.h2: Recording fees at the Terrebonne Parish Clerk of Court
sections.html:
A Houma sale is recorded with the Terrebonne Parish Clerk of Court. Fees start at $105 for one to five pages. Call the clerk to confirm the current schedule before closing.

Document lengthFee, one index type
1 to 5 pages$105
6 to 25 pages$205
26 to 50 pages$305
51 or more pages$305 plus $5 per extra page

The fee includes up to 10 names indexed, a certified copy and the portal fee, and it is charged separately for each recording book. Under the Civil Code a sale of an immovable must be made by authentic act or by act under private signature, so you sign the act of sale before a notary and it is then recorded.

sections.h2: From offer to closing in Houma
sections.html:
After you accept an offer, the notary or closing attorney orders a title search and asks your lender for a payoff. Gather your deed, insurance and repair records, any elevation certificate and your latest tax bill. At the signing, your loan balance, unpaid taxes and recording fees come out of the proceeds, and the act of sale then goes to the clerk. If the house still carries storm damage, tell the buyer what you know and hand over the repair paperwork, since that protects you if a question comes up later.

Timing depends on the route. A financed buyer adds an appraisal, an inspection and lender conditions, and any open repair item can slow or stall the loan. A cash buyer skips those steps, so closing is limited mainly by the title search and the notary's calendar. In both cases, ask for the settlement statement a few days ahead and read it line by line, so any unexpected charge gets resolved before you sign.

sections.h2: Which way of selling a Houma house makes sense?
sections.html:
The choice usually comes down to repairs, timing and who pays for them. A cash sale as-is helps a house that still needs storm repairs or a roof, while a traditional listing may suit a finished house that can wait for financing and an appraisal.

Whichever route you take, read the contract and any cancellation language first, and write down the net amount you need after the payoff and costs so you can compare offers fairly. A listing may bring a higher price but takes longer and demands repairs and showings. A cash offer is usually lower, yet it can close on a date you choose and leaves the roof, drywall and mold questions with the buyer. Houma owners who left after the storm and are managing a distant property often value that certainty most.

faqs.q: Is Houma its own city government?
faqs.a: Houma remains a city, but its government was absorbed by the parish in 1984. Planning and permits run through the Terrebonne Parish Consolidated Government.

faqs.q: What are Houma's flood maps doing?
faqs.a: FEMA released revised preliminary flood maps for portions of Houma and unincorporated Terrebonne Parish on October 8, 2021. Check the effective and preliminary status for your address with the local floodplain administrator or FEMA's Map Service Center.

faqs.q: Where is a deed recorded in Houma?
faqs.a: At the Terrebonne Parish Clerk of Court. Fees start at $105 for one to five pages, including up to 10 names indexed, a certified copy and the portal fee. Call the clerk to confirm current fees.

faqs.q: How many Houma homes are owner-occupied?
faqs.a: 72.4 percent of housing units for 2020 to 2024, with a median home value of $205,900. These are citywide figures.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Houma house that still has Ida damage?
faqs.a: Yes, as-is sales are possible. Tell buyers what you know about the damage and keep insurance and repair records. A cash buyer is not working under a lender's repair conditions, which is why damaged houses are often sold this way.
